title: Judge Blocks Trump's 250-Foot Washington Arch Hours After Panel Approves It
excerpt: Judge Tanya Chutkan paused all construction at Memorial Circle for 14 days after the planning commission's 8-4 approval, in the fight over whether Congress ever authorised the monument.
body:
• A federal judge blocked construction of President Donald Trump's proposed 250-foot triumphal arch in Washington, DC, for 14 days, less than two hours after a federal planning commission approved it 8-4 late on November 5.
  • US District Judge Tanya Chutkan granted the temporary restraining order sought by the District of Columbia and Virginia, barring any construction, excavation or land disturbance at Memorial Circle.
  • The legal fight turns on authorisation: DC, Virginia and a group of Vietnam War veterans argue Congress never approved the arch; the administration says Congress authorised it more than a century ago.
  • What it means for you: no building work can start for at least 14 days, and the administration must certify compliance to the court by November 9 — anyone using Memorial Bridge should still expect protest and hearing-related disruption, not construction, in that window.

A federal judge blocked construction of President Donald Trump's proposed triumphal arch in Washington, DC, on the night of November 5, granting a 14-day temporary restraining order less than two hours after the National Capital Planning Commission had given the project its final approval in an 8-4 vote, NPR reported.

The arch would stand 250 feet tall in Memorial Circle, the traffic island on the bridge linking the Lincoln Memorial to Arlington National Cemetery, across the Potomac River from the Lincoln Memorial. Modelled on Paris's Arc de Triomphe, it would stand more than 80 feet taller than its French counterpart and rise to nearly the height of the 288-foot US Capitol, according to USA Today.

An eight-hour hearing, then two opposite decisions

The commission's virtual meeting began at 1 p.m. and heard nearly eight hours of testimony, with 131 people signed up to speak, NPR reported. Most opposed the arch: veterans and their relatives, Democratic lawmakers, historic preservation experts and residents raised its legality, its cost, the view it would obstruct, and its effect on Arlington National Cemetery and on Washington's complicated airspace. Only a handful of speakers, including Republican Reps. Andrew Clyde of Georgia and Brian Mast of Florida, both veterans, supported it.

A motion by DC Council Chair Phil Mendelson to postpone the vote until final site and building plans were submitted failed 4-8. The commission then approved the arch. The Trump administration, which had told the court it could begin excavation the same day, notified the court within half an hour — a step Judge Tanya Chutkan had required in advance, setting up the late-night ruling. Her order, laid out in a 33-page opinion, bars the government from "initiating, making or otherwise effectuating" any construction-related activity near the site, NPR reported, and USA Today noted it covers excavation, demolition, land disturbance, utility installation and roadway closures at Memorial Circle on Columbus Island. The administration must update the court by November 9 and certify compliance.

The legal argument at the centre

The mechanism of the dispute is authorisation. This is not a ruling on whether an arch is desirable; it is a fight over who gets to approve a permanent monument in the capital. A group of Vietnam War veterans and an architectural historian sued earlier this year arguing an arch is unlawful without congressional approval, which the administration has not sought. DC and Virginia filed a similar suit last weekend — dated October 31 in USA Today's account — calling the project "legally indefensible." Chutkan consolidated the cases.

The administration's answer, as commissioners supporting the project put it, is that Congress authorised the site in 1925 when it approved a pair of 166-foot columns on Memorial Circle that were never built, and more broadly, per USA Today, that Congress approved the arch when it authorised the bridge across the Potomac more than a century ago. Chutkan scrutinised the administration's shifting justifications, including a late emphasis on national security — Trump said on November 2 the arch could house drones and snipers — and agreed the local governments were likely to be harmed once work began, including by immediate traffic disruption from work officials said would run 20 hours a day for two to three years.

"It's right smack in the middle of everything, so very important for our military. But from a beautification standpoint, it'll be the most beautiful arch in the world."

— Donald Trump, President of the United States

What happens next

For the next 14 days, nothing gets built. The Justice Department has said an initial six to eight months of excavation and foundation work could have begun within days; above-ground construction would start in May 2027 at the earliest, in a project lasting 33 to 39 months in total, according to reporting cited by NPR. Whether any of that survives depends on the courts — and possibly on the new Congress. Rep. Don Beyer of Virginia has introduced a bill to prohibit and defund the arch, and Democratic lawmakers have said they intend to pursue the issue when they take their majority in January, NPR reported. Full coverage is at NPR and CNN.
